"Furthermore, without altering the previous seal, bend the two middle fingers into the binding and extend the two thumbs upright in the form of a vajra; this is called the Seal of the Vajra of Sublime Joy."

Furthermore, without changing the previous mudrā, form hooks with the two middle fingers and assume the posture of heroic advance, placing it at the center of one's own heart; this is called the Mahāsukha-vajra-mudrā.

From this mudrā, four mudrās arise. That is to say: from the previously mentioned vajra-bond, extend the two index fingers like hooks; bend the two middle fingers and the two thumbs into the palms with their pads facing one another, forming the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Vajranetra.
"Furthermore, without altering the previous mudrā, touch the two thumbs together to form the mudrā of Vajracarcikā Bodhisattva.
Again, without altering the previous mudrā, extend all the fingers inward and erect the index fingers to form the mudrā of Vajraketu Bodhisattva."
Furthermore, without altering the previous mudrā, form the gesture of power by placing the hands between the two thighs; this constitutes the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Vajrarāgīśvara.
Again, the dharmapada-mudrā is explained:
first, take the syllable *HŪṂ* as a sublime melodic chant, and subsequently proclaim the vidyā-mantra of the Dharma-jñāna-mudrā, which is as follows:

"Hūṃ ha ā. Furthermore, the various *karmamudrās* are taught: herein, first, one forms the *vajrabandha* with both hands; the two index fingers are shaped like hooks, the two ring fingers are inserted into the palms, and the two thumbs are placed over them to form the Great Samaya Fist Mudrā.
Having bound this mudrā, one further produces from the two fists—the karma-muṣṭi and the vajra-muṣṭi—the high-lifting mudrā of the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva.
"As for that mudrā: first, with both hands, form the vajra-fists; then, assume the posture of a hero discharging an arrow, followed by the postures of raising a banner and lifting it aloft."
Thereafter, with the vajra-fist whirling like lightning, he rises and circles about, then performs playful gestures (*līlā*).

With both hands forming a powerful, tight *añjali* mudrā, he holds flowers and other offerings; first placing them upon his crown, he gradually lowers them while assuming playful postures, successively presenting various offerings. Finally, he performs the secret offering of the vajra dance (*vajranṛtya*).
Furthermore, performing the playful gesture and the vajra-raising posture while executing a whirling motion, one gazes upon and prostrates to all the worthy sages and saints.
This mudrā is also called the Great Samaya-mahāmudrā; it is capable of accomplishing all non-empty activities.
Furthermore, the Great Sovereign Seal of the Vajra Realm of the Supreme Body of all Tathāgatas is proclaimed:

First, perform the fearless posture (abhaya-āsana) with the body held straight and upright; then, with both hands, form the Vajra-bond of all Tathāgatas, extend the two index fingers like hooks, and subsequently spread them apart; those two index fingers, appearing like a halo, constitute the seal.
Furthermore, the Vajra-mudrā is explained:

born from all vajras, this mudrā first forms the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), then forms the vajra-bind (*vajrabandha*). This bind faces outward like the established form of the original samādhi-vajra. Subsequently, from within the vajra-bind of Vajrasattva and the others, the various fingers emerge; with the two index fingers forming the vajra-sign, one completes the mudrā.
"Furthermore, making the gesture of holding a sword with strength with the right hand is called the Vajra-Sādhu-mudrā.
Furthermore, interlocking the backs of the tips of all the fingers is called the Ratna-mudrā."
"Furthermore, without changing the previous mudrā, insert all the fingers into the center; this is called the Vajra Flame Mudrā.

Furthermore, without changing the previous mudrā, form the 'vajra-lotus' joined palms with the motion of turning a robe, then insert the fingers into the palms and subsequently spread them apart; this is called the Wheel Mudrā."
"Furthermore, without altering the previous mudrā, these same index fingers and so forth are also called the Finger-Wheel Mudrā (Aṅgulicakra-mudrā).
Again, without altering the previous mudrā, forming the Vajra-Palm is called the Birth Mudrā (Utpatti-mudrā)."
"Furthermore, forming the two index fingers like hooks is called the Central Vajra Seal (Madhyama-vajramudrā).
Furthermore, pressing the two index fingers inward against the two thumbs is called the Samaya-vajra-fist Seal (Samaya-vajramuṣṭi-mudrā)."
"Furthermore, with both hands, form the vajra-fists according to the original rite; this is called the Karma-baṃdha mudrā.
Next, the heart-mudrās of the various bodhisattvas are proclaimed:
herein, first form the Tathāgata-fist with the right hand and the wrathful finger with the left hand; this is called the Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva mudrā."
"Furthermore, forming the vajra-anger finger gesture with both hands and the two little fingers in the shape of a sword is called the Vajraratna-mudrā.
Again, forming the four-gate gesture with the two index fingers and the two thumbs is called the Abhiṣeka-mudrā."

Furthermore, with both hands forming a tight *añjali*, extend the two little fingers and the two index fingers so that they resemble the form of a four-petaled lotus; this is called the Great Lotus Seal (*Mahāpadma-mudrā*).
"Furthermore, in this context, bending [the fingers] so they enter the thumb is called the Tathāgata Fist.
Extending the index finger upright is called the Vajra Fist.
If the index finger is used in the form of a sword or a ring, it is also called the 'Excellent' (Sādhu) Seal."
Alternatively, it may take the form of a jewel and is also called the "Flame-Arising Seal.
Furthermore, forming vajra-fists with both hands, with the left thumb extended upward and the right hand in the gesture of three banners, it is called the "Three-Banners Seal."
"Again, pressing the thumb of the right hand against the nail of the middle finger is called the Caturdik-cakravarti-mudrā (Mudrā of the Four-Directional Wheel-Turning King).
Again, grasping the five fingers of the left hand with the right hand is called the Akṣamālā-mudrā (Mudrā of the Rosary)."

Again, with both hands, perform the gestures of play, garlands, song, and dance, letting them fall from behind the crown of the head; then, place the index fingers of both hands in the palms, extend the remaining fingers, and touch them to one another—this is called the *hastasaṃsparśa-mudrā* (the Hand-Touching Seal).
"Again, form fists with both hands; extend the two index fingers like hooks and interlace the two little fingers, turning them outward. This is called the Seal of the Sharp Fangs."
Furthermore, regarding the ritual application of the *karmas* among the various *cittamudrās*:

whenever the practitioner forms any of these *cittamudrās*, they should recite the great mantra (*mahāvidyā*) of their respective family once. They should then enter into correspondence with the wisdom of the recollection of the deity (*devatā-anusmṛti-jñāna*), and subsequently seek accomplishment according to their capacity.

When seeking accomplishment within all such ritual manuals (*kalpa*), one should daily perform the mudrās according to the prescribed method; thereby, one shall immediately attain all supreme accomplishments.
"Furthermore, the general mudrās applicable to all teachings are proclaimed:
herein, there are four types of bodily mudrās: first, the *vikṣepa* (the vigorous gesture);
second, the *ākarṣaṇa* (the summoning gesture); third, the *āveśakara* (the gesture for causing possession); and fourth, the *pradānakara* (the gesture for making offerings)."
If one binds these four mudrās, one can perform all rites of veneration, summoning, and the destruction of evil; success will be attained in a single instant.
"There are four kinds of speech-mudrās (*vāg-mudrā*); these are the vidyā-mantras of the Dharma-knowledge-mudrā, namely:
*Aḥ hūṃ hūṃ jaḥ*. These mudrās and mantras can accomplish all rites of *āveśa* [possession] and other such siddhis."
“There are four kinds of heart-seals (*cittamudrā*):

first, with a single mind, to enter universally into all bodies and extensively perform acts of veneration and love; second, to be able to gather in the minds of others; third, to accomplish all beneficial purposes; and fourth, to pacify and eliminate all sufferings. These four seals are capable of producing the four kinds of accomplishments mentioned above.”
"Furthermore, there are also four kinds of Vajra-mudrās, namely:

with the vajra-fist, first, raising; second, lowering; third, striking; and fourth, holding. These four mudrās can perform all manner of actions, such as lifting up, casting down, destroying, and annihilating."
“The Gazing Mudrās are also of four kinds: first, the playful, laughing gaze of the raised vajra;

second, the twinkling, momentary gaze of radiant light; third, the frowning, intensely fierce and wrathful gaze; and fourth, the unblinking, steadfast gaze of both eyes. These four mudrās can eliminate all sufferings such as malarial poisons and demonic possessions.”
"Furthermore, among all mudrās, if one binds the Great Mudrā (mahāmudrā), one immediately attains the supreme accomplishment.

As for that Great Mudrā, it refers to the Great Mudrā of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great Mudrā of the Vajra-Subjugation of all Tathāgatas, the Great Mudrā of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Great Mudrā of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha... this very Great Mudrā is also the Samaya Mudrā."
"Regarding this *vajrapāṇi-samaya-viparyāsa-mudrā*, it is as explained in the original ritual (*vidhi*).

Furthermore, form two *vajra-fists*: first, extend the index finger of the left fist outward and point it upward; place the right fist inward at the heart. This is called the *sarvatathāgata-samaya-viparyāsa-mudrā*."

Furthermore, first bend the right arm into the shape of a ring; with the left hand, extend the index finger upward to form the mudrā of making a pact. This is called the Vajra-Subjugation Samādhi Asura-mudrā.

Furthermore, with both hands forming a tight *añjali*, the two little fingers and the two thumbs are spread apart like the appearance of a four-petaled lotus; this is called the Samaya-mudrā of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva within the Lotus Family.

Furthermore, with both hands forming the vajra-bond (*vajrabandha*), let the two index fingers and thumbs hang downward in the manner of opening four gates; arising from the heart of samādhi, one abides at the gate of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). This is called the *asādhāraṇa-mudrā* (special seal) of the Samādhi of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
Furthermore, for each of these, there is a Dharma-knowledge seal-mantra (*vidyā*), namely:
*HŪṂ Ā HŪṂ HRĪḤ TĀLAṂ*. One should form the *karma-samaya* seal according to the original ritual procedure.
Furthermore, regarding the *karmamudrā* of the heart-seals (*cittamudrā*) of all bodhisattvas:
herein, the *karmamudrā* of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi is the *vajramuṣṭi*.

Within the Tathāgata family, the *karmamudrā* of all Tathāgatas is formed by bending the fingers of the aforementioned *vajramuṣṭi* into the palm and placing them between the thumb; this is called the *tathāgatamuṣṭi*.
Within the Vajra Family, the Vajra Fist is formed by extending the index fingers to make a threatening gesture; this is called the Vajra Fist.
Within the Lotus Family, the Lotus Fist is formed by placing the thumbs side-by-side and pressing them against the nails of the middle fingers; this is called the Lotus Fist.

Within the Jewel Family, the Jewel Fist is formed according to the ritual procedures for the Great Jewel Samādhi Fist and the Vajra-Jewel Fist; once bound according to the dharma, it is called the Jewel Fist.
"Regarding all other seals to be employed, they should be bound according to the insignia specified in the various ritual manuals.
This answers the seventh question.
"As for what is called the accomplishment of the seal (mudrā-siddhi):"
"Every day at the early dawn, the practitioner should bind the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) to seek accomplishment.

Reciting the root heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*) of the deity according to the ritual method one hundred times, they should thereafter recite the minor mantra (*upahṛdaya*). All activities should be performed according to the ritual method."
"Furthermore, by chanting the syllable HŪṂ with a melodious song, one attains the accomplishment of the mudrā in an instant.
This answers the eighth question.
"As for what is called 'secret offering':..."
"In the great secret offering of song and dance, the practitioner of Vajrasattva—
whether increasing or decreasing as appropriate— will achieve all that is done and obtain sublime bliss."
Furthermore, regarding what is called "Vajra Offering," as described in those various teachings:
by rotating upward and downward and then gazing again, all sentient beings attain accomplishment.
This answers the ninth question.
Regarding what is called "the accomplishment of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity)":
"If all sentient beings in the world / Seek accomplishment at all times,"
"One should always maintain the recitation for the sake of benefiting others, in accordance with the dharma of one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).
This answers the tenth question.
Regarding what was said about "recitation" and "dharma applications":
"The practitioner should not move the tip of the tongue, and should further cause the lips and teeth to meet;
one should recite according to the ritual procedures found in the various teachings, remaining free from the speech of Vajra."
He utters a profound and wondrous sound like the beat of a drum; this is the dhāraṇī-recitation method of the Buddha Family.
The Dharma-Cloud Thunder-Sound of the Vajra Family produces the subtle and wondrous speech born of the Vajra lineage.
The speech of samādhi belongs to the Lotus Family; according to its instructions and ritual procedures, all secret and wondrous melodic sounds are themselves the vajra-speech of sublime bliss.
The various sections contain one hundred recitations; within the methods of summoning there are twenty-one.
As explained in the supreme teachings, one should never grow weary but constantly perform the recitation.
This answers the eleventh question.
As for what was asked:
"Who cannot achieve accomplishment in the Dharma?"
"Thus it is said:
'Just as I, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, am the gateway of great bliss through which all are revered and loved,
and from whom all dharmas are born— those who are impure shall not achieve accomplishment.'"
This answers the twelfth question.
As for what was said:
"How can those with meager merit achieve accomplishment?"
"Those [who enter] these maṇḍalas, supreme and peerless, should simply follow the ritual procedures.
Even those who have committed sins and possess little merit shall attain accomplishment in this very life."
This answers the thirteenth question.
"This is called the Supreme Ritual within all rituals of the Great King of Teachings of the Great Samaya.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, further receiving the instructions of all the Tathāgatas, addressed the assembly of devas, including Brahmā, Śakra, and others, speaking these words:
“O sons of the gods!

Within this great ritual manual, you should each likewise proclaim your own heart-mantras (*hṛdaya*). According to what is thus proclaimed, you shall bring about various accomplishments throughout the long night, extensively benefiting all sentient beings.”

Having spoken these words, the assembly of devas all rejoiced; leaping for joy and feeling exultant, their hearts were filled with delight. Immediately, they together circumambulated the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and all the other Tathāgatas, keeping them to their right, and each joined their palms in reverent prostration.
Again, having prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, they each spoke their own heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra) in succession.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, first spoke his heart-mantra: “Oṃ vajramuṣṭi-sarvakuṇṭha.

“If there is a practitioner who, according to the ritual, recites this heart-mantra of mine one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*), that person will immediately attain the supreme accomplishment of the Divine Net (*divyapañjara*). Furthermore, they will be able to summon rain and also stop rain; they will also be able to suppress and eliminate all thunder, hail, lightning, and the like. They will be victorious in all battles, and even all seeds and crops will flourish and increase.”
"This is called the Ritual Manual of Śakra-devendra.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, spoke this heart-mantra:

“Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ | Satat satavidurivāriṇan | Parivunidvakhya-dhimahi-tiyu | Yuna-prajñāna-ya-tu | (1) “If there is a practitioner who recites this heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*) of mine according to the ritual rules for one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*), that person will be able to perform the rites of pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), and summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*). All their undertakings shall be perfectly fulfilled, and they shall also achieve success in all *homā* rituals.”
"This is called the Ritual Manual of the Great Brahmā King.
At that time, the Lord Nārāyaṇa spoke this heart-mantra:

"Oṃ māyājāla-saṃdarśaya sarvanamanā hūṃ. "If there is a practitioner who, according to the ritual, recites this heart-mantra of mine one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*), that person will be able to enter the palace of the asuras, manifest all manner of illusory transformations and such, and perform all methods of subjugation."
Once one has recited this heart-mantra ten thousand times (one lakṣa), one will attain great sovereignty within the world.
This is called the Ritual Manual of Nārāyaṇa.
At that time, Maheśvara, the Lord of all the three realms, spoke this heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*):

"Oṃ tiri sarvasarvaskandha mahālaulyasattvasādya hūṃ. "If there is a practitioner who, according to the ritual, recites this heart-mantra of mine one hundred thousand times, that person shall attain accomplishment in all worldly dharmas."

If one recites this heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*) amidst all types of beings, one is able to summon them all, or bind them, or cause *āveśa* (possession), or effect subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*); or cause them to come, or send them away; or cause them to tremble, or make them dance and sing; or cause them to become bewildered, or destroy their wealth and possessions, even down to all objects of enjoyment, so that they may be obtained entirely and used at will. Among all the hosts of *mātṛkā* goddesses, one becomes invincible; among all maṇḍalas, one becomes an *ācārya*. One can perform all activities according to one’s will, and once the practice is perfected, all the most supreme methods of accomplishment (*siddhi*) shall be attained.
At that time, the assembly of devaputras of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven spoke this heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*):

"Oṃ sarvaratirāgasiñce. "If there is a practitioner who, according to the ritual, recites this heart-mantra of mine for one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*), they shall immediately gain the faith and deep respect of all goddesses and asura maidens; they shall attain mastery and delight among all *siddhis*; furthermore, they shall be constantly loved and honored by all people, and shall attain sovereignty within the heavens."
At that time, the entire assembly of goddesses spoke this heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*):

“Oṃ rativilāsa sarvakāmuka karmakarama rāmaya huṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ. “If there is a practitioner who recites this heart-mantra of mine according to the ritual once, that person shall immediately gain great love and respect from all *aprasara* [spirits]. Furthermore, whatever the practitioner desires in their heart, those beings will come at once to bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*).”
"If four years have been completed, he will perform acts of endearment for the present body, and all other undertakings shall be fully accomplished.
He further spoke of the Great Maṇḍala where the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven assemble:
"It should be known that this is the mundane ritual; all other dharmas are the supreme accomplishment methods of Amoghasiddhi."

The form of that maṇḍala should be drawn according to the ritual rules as having four sides and four gates, adorned all around with various jewel trees, with banners, victory standards, and exquisite jewel canopies erected; furthermore, it should be extensively decorated with the celestial *udyāna* (pleasure garden) trees and *kovidāra* trees.

Within that, one further draws the palace of Śakra; in its center is seated the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, surrounded by the sixteen great bodhisattvas, arranged according to their respective positions in accordance with the ritual rules. Outside the maṇḍala, one further arranges the hosts of devas and other deities in successive order.

Having thus arranged the maṇḍala, the Vajrācārya forms the mudrā according to the ritual: first, he makes vajra-fists with both hands; then, he interlocks the two little fingers and the two thumbs, gradually raising them to form the Vajra-water mudrā.

Furthermore, taking a sublime flower and entering the maṇḍala, one should cast the flower according to the ritual procedure; thereafter, reciting the great vidyā-mantra of the respective family once, one is able to summon Vajrasattva and all other noble deities.
Thereafter, have the disciple likewise follow the previous ritual: forming the mudrā and holding the flower, enter the maṇḍala.
Having entered, cast the flower; the place where the flower falls is that of the *iṣṭadevatā*.
Thereafter, the ācārya confers the samaya verse, saying:
“The Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—the Triple Gem— And likewise the Vajradhara Lord:
Always practice with a heart of reverence and filial piety according to your ability, And you shall achieve all that you desire.”
Having spoken these verses, he further declared:
"From this day forward, all that you do shall be accomplished.
This is called the Great Maṇḍala of the Assembled Assembly of the Thirty-three Heavens.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, having proclaimed before all the Tathāgatas the profound dharma-gate of the aforementioned Secret Great King of Teachings, further spoke these verses for the benefit of all sentient beings:
"For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, And to cause all teachings to be accomplished,
I proclaim this Secret Great King of Teachings, The synthesized dharma of the Great Samaya."
If there are those who seek accomplishment, they should always give rise to pure faith;
then that Great Vajradhara King will constantly abide upon their crown to provide protection.
Whatever the practitioner desires to enjoy, may it always be obtained as wished;
furthermore, protection is provided, so that all sufferings are completely eliminated, and because they are guarded, no obstacles shall arise.
All the matters of accomplishment that have been taught, for the benefit of all sentient beings of the future—
whether through the ear, the tongue, or in dreams— may Vajrapāṇi grant his constant protection.
May all that is sought be swiftly fulfilled; may the great secret samādhi be universally gathered;
and may one obtain the state of all Buddhas and noble sages, constantly bestowing all methods of accomplishment.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi had spoken these various secret dharmas, all the Tathāgatas together praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
At that time, the entire great assembly rejoiced greatly, accepted it with faith, and practiced accordingly.
This concludes the fourth fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-guhyasamāja-mahātantrarāja-sūtra*.
